name: Fluridil
lead: Fluridil (marketed in Europe as Eucapil, and also known as topilutamide) is a topical antiandrogen that people apply to the scalp with the aim of keeping or thickening hair in androgenetic alopecia, so that the hairline and crown look fuller. Its developers describe it as a rationally designed agent that suppresses the human androgen receptor locally, is highly hydrophobic, breaks down by hydrolysis and is not absorbed systemically.[1]

Wikipedia reports that topilutamide was introduced for medical use in 2003 and is marketed by Interpharma Praha as a 2 percent scalp formulation, available in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, with the patent expiring in 2020. It is described as cosmetic use in Europe and has no FDA or EMA approval for androgenetic alopecia.[4] Because it blocks the receptor rather than inhibiting 5-alpha-reductase, it works differently from finasteride and dutasteride.[1][4]

The published clinical evidence is a single early study: a 2002 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 43 men with androgenetic alopecia, reported alongside a patch-test safety study in 20 men.[1] The trial reported an increase in the proportion of hairs in the anagen (growth) phase, and no changes in sexual function, libido, blood counts or blood chemistry.[1] No larger or independent trials were found. On T Nation, fluridil is mentioned occasionally as a lesser-known option beside RU58841.[2][3]
infobox: Cosmetic use in Europe; no FDA or EMA approval for androgenetic alopecia[4]

paras: According to the researchers who developed it, fluridil is a rationally designed topical antiandrogen that suppresses the human androgen receptor. It is highly hydrophobic and hydrolytically degradable, and the authors describe it as systemically non-resorbable. In animal studies they reported high local and general tolerance.[1] Because it acts on the receptor rather than on 5-alpha-reductase, it is mechanistically distinct from finasteride and dutasteride. Wikipedia reports that fluridil binds the androgen receptor with about 9 to 15 times higher affinity than older antiandrogens such as bicalutamide and hydroxyflutamide, though it says more research is needed to validate this; in human serum it degrades with a half-life of about 6 hours and neither it nor its metabolites were detectable in human studies.[4]

In the 2002 trial, 43 men with androgenetic alopecia (Norwood grade II to Va) used 2 percent fluridil or placebo. Baseline anagen and telogen counts were equal in all groups. After three months the average anagen percentage was unchanged in placebo subjects but rose from 76 percent to 85 percent in fluridil subjects and to 87 percent at nine months. Former placebo subjects who then received fluridil rose from 76 to 85 percent after six months.[1] The abstract reports phototrichogram-based hair-cycle outcomes; the sources reviewed do not describe hair counts, density or cosmetic ratings from independent trials.

Topilutamide was introduced for medical use in 2003 and is sold as Eucapil by Interpharma Praha, with marketing limited to the Czech Republic and Slovakia according to Wikipedia; its patent expired in 2020. The article lists a former developmental code name, BP-766.[4]

In the patch-test arm, 20 men received occlusive forearm patches with 2, 4 and 6 percent fluridil, isopropanol and vaseline over 21 days; neither fluridil nor isopropanol showed sensitisation or irritation potential, unlike vaseline.[1] In the main trial, sexual function, libido, haematology and blood chemistry were reported as normal, and blood analysis for fluridil itself was included.[1] The trial was small and short, and long-term safety data are not available in the sources reviewed.

Fluridil appears in T Nation hair-loss threads as an option alongside RU58841 and other topical antiandrogens, with users describing it as lesser known; one poster says that for someone on testosterone, its 'cost to benefit ratio nose-dives' relative to other choices, and another says they 'haven't learned much about this one yet'.[2][3]

One randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical study (43 men with androgenetic alopecia) and a 20-man patch-test study were published in 2002, reporting increased anagen percentage and no sexual, haematological or biochemical changes.[1] No other human trials were found in the sources reviewed.

claims.claim: Fluridil is a topical antiandrogen option for hair loss that avoids systemic effects
claims.believers: Forum users list it among hair-loss options and note it is sold as Eucapil, though one says it is an option whose cost-to-benefit ratio is poorer than other choices.[2][3]
claims.experts: The only published human trial (43 men, 2002) reported increased anagen percentage and normal sexual function, hematology and chemistry, with the authors describing the drug as not systemically absorbed; independent replication has not been found.[1]

card.summary: Obscure topical antiandrogen (Eucapil) for hair loss, backed by a single small 2002 trial.
card.note: Only one small randomised trial is known; it was reported by its developers and has not been independently replicated in the sources reviewed.

quick.overview:
Fluridil is a topical antiandrogen sold in Europe as Eucapil for androgenetic alopecia. It is meant to block androgen receptors locally in the scalp rather than lowering hormones throughout the body.

The published evidence is a single 2002 randomised trial in 43 men, which reported a rise in anagen-phase hair percentage over placebo and no changes in sexual function or lab values.
quick.mechanism: Fluridil is described by its developers as suppressing the human androgen receptor while being highly hydrophobic, easily degraded by hydrolysis and not absorbed into the body.
quick.risks: The 2002 study found no irritation or sensitisation in patch tests and normal sexual function and blood values, but it was small and short, and long-term data are not available. It is not an approved drug in the US.

angle.text: Fluridil is used on the scalp to keep more hairs in the growth phase by blocking androgen receptors where hair loss occurs. The only trial reported a higher percentage of growing hairs on phototrichogram.
